bill.title: A bill to amend title 18, United States Code, to provide that officers and employees of the executive branch are required to recuse themselves in matters affecting the financial interests of their previous employers, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would require executive branch officers and employees to recuse themselves from matters that affect the financial interests of their previous employers. It amends federal criminal law to establish this recusal requirement. The bill aims to address potential conflicts of interest when government officials handle issues involving companies or organizations they recently worked for.

industries.rationale: The bill creates new recusal obligations that would affect how law firms and lobbying firms place former employees in government roles and manage conflicts.
Financial institutions frequently employ individuals who move into regulatory and policy roles, making recusal requirements directly relevant to their engagement with government.
Pharmaceutical companies regularly see former employees enter FDA and HHS positions where recusal from matters affecting former employers would limit their scope of work.
Defense contractors frequently hire from and send employees to the Department of Defense and related agencies, making recusal rules material to procurement and policy processes.
Technology companies employ individuals who move into regulatory and policy positions where recusal from matters affecting former employers would constrain their activities.

plain.everydayEffect: Nothing has changed yet. The title alone does not say what would change for you, and this tool will not guess. Most bills never become law.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.
Lawyers & Lobbyists is also the top donor sector for 2 other members from CA. That points to the industry being big in the state, not to anything about this member.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
